page.label: The Rainbow Bridge from Along the River During the Qingming Festival, rebuilt in 3D, with a porter you can walk across it and a camera that goes all the way round
page.description: The Rainbow Bridge from Along the River During the Qingming Festival, rebuilt in 3D from the painting: walk a porter across it and go all the way round.
text: The river and its banks are the painting itself, laid back down on the ground it shows: from the painter’s own direction they line up with the scroll exactly. The bridge, the boats, the halls, houses, sheds, stalls, tables and umbrellas along both banks are rebuilt as simple models dressed in their own painted timbers and roofs, so you can walk round them.

The people are the painting’s own: the crowd on the bridge, the street at the bridge’s foot, the porters on a boat and the trackers hauling another, each cut out of the scroll and stood up where they are painted, with the carts, horses, donkeys and willows beside them. The painting only ever shows one side of things, so a model’s far side wears its near side, mirrored, and where the painting is hidden behind something the gap is filled with its own blank water and silk.

Your walker is a porter with two baskets on a shoulder pole, borrowed from the street outside Dr. Zhao’s shop near the end of the scroll. He can go anywhere on the bridge and the banks around it, but not into the river or through a building; hold Shift to hurry. He, and everyone else, turns to face you like a paper cut-out.

The near miss is staged from what the painting shows at its moment; how it got there is imagined. The sounds are synthesized, not recorded. The notes quote Meng Yuanlao’s memoir of Kaifeng, 东京梦华录 (1147).

pois.title: The Rainbow Bridge
pois.body: Meng Yuanlao’s memoir of Kaifeng, written in 1147 after the city was lost, describes it: no piers, only great timbers spanning the river, painted red, “like a flying rainbow”. With nothing standing in the water, boats could pass right under it.

pois.title: The big boat
pois.body: The largest boat in this stretch, swinging toward the arch with its mast still coming down. Readers have long felt the danger here, and Yu Hui of the Palace Museum counts the near collision among the scroll’s quiet warnings.

pois.title: Stalls on the deck
pois.body: Peddlers have set up on the bridge itself, under awnings and umbrellas, and everyone else squeezes past them. In the painting the deck is as crowded as any street.

pois.title: The wine shop
pois.body: Its signs read 十千脚店: “ten thousand”, probably from an old line of verse praising wine at ten thousand cash a measure, and jiaodian, a smaller shop that bought its wine from one of the city’s great licensed taverns. Meng Yuanlao wrote that every wine shop in the capital tied a festive gateway of poles like this one at its door.
link: A great licensed tavern, on the scroll

pois.title: Trackers
pois.body: A team hauls a boat upstream on a towline made fast high on its mast, leaning into it a step at a time.
link: Boats on the Bian River, on the scroll

pois.title: An open restaurant
pois.body: On the near bank, diners sit at tables under a broad tiled roof, open to the street and the river.

haul.about: the trackers lean into the towline step by step and the boat surges against it
